title: Chat runtime sandbox quickstart + reconnect playbook
summary: Intro + live sandbox handoff of Redwood hosted chat API. Covered streaming behavior, key params (max_tokens, temperature, stop, top_p), reconnect/retry patterns, idempotency and token accounting. Discussed cost/latency tradeoffs, KV prefix caching, and a short demo of fallback to a smaller model when latency spikes. Agreed next steps: send sandbox access, share retry pattern examples, run a small latency benchmark with Clearline data, and schedule a technical deep dive for private deployment options.

transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-04-16 15:00 PDT — 48m — Attendees: Liam (Redwood AE), Sofia (Redwood SE), Marcus (Redwood SE), Maya (Clearline ML), Tom (Clearline CTO), Priya (Product), Evan (SRE)

[00:00] Liam (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro — I'm Liam, AE on the Redwood side, joined by Sofia and Marcus. We're gonna run through a short hosted API sandbox demo focused on streaming behavior, tuning a couple params, and a reconnect/retry playbook.

[00:18] Tom (Clearline): Thanks, yeah we only have about 45 minutes so, appreciate the focused agenda. We're particularly interested in predictable latency for chat flows and cost controls.

[00:30] Sofia (Redwood SE): Awesome. Quick question — what stack are you running for the front end and the server side? Are you calling from a browser or through a backend?

[00:40] Maya (Clearline ML): Mostly backend Node services, a mixture of Express + some serverless lambdas. We also have a mobile client but the initial traffic is server-proxied.

[00:47] Sofia: Great, that maps well to the typical patterns we'll demo. We'll show streaming from the hosted endpoint (text-stream) and then talk about partial reconnects and idempotency tokens for safe retries.

[01:10] Marcus (Redwood SE): Just to set expectations — streaming sends token deltas over an open connection. If the connection drops we recommend a reconnect using the same conversation id and the idempotency key to ask for the missing tail. There's a small window where you may re-receive tokens so the client should handle duplicate trimming.

[01:38] Evan (Clearline SRE): So the idempotency key — is that per-request or per-conversation chunk? How does token accounting work so we don't double-bill?

[01:48] Sofia: Good call. Idempotency is per generation request. Redwood uses a request-id header you can set; if you retry within a short retention window we dedupe at the platform and only bill once for identical generations. For partial reconnects where you fetch a missing suffix, we have short-lived KV cache for the prefix so the runtime can continue the sequence without re-generating large prefixes. Billing is on final tokens emitted — but if you explicitly re-generate with a different prompt it's billed separately.

[02:20] Priya (Product): Can you show the actual params we should tune? We need a simple cheat sheet for product folks.

[02:29] Liam: Sure, live demo — switching to the sandbox console. (brief pause, screen share) You'll see the chat endpoint playground with a default model pinned. Key params: max_tokens, temperature, top_p, presence_penalty, frequency_penalty, and the stop sequences. Also a streaming param called chunk_size/stream_interval on the client side.

[02:58] [03:00] Sofia: I'm going to send a quick example request — Node snippet — so you can see reconnect logic. (typing)

[03:15] Speaker 1 (Recording glitch): uh-huh, looks good, yeah

[03:22] Sofia: Example pseudocode: open stream, set request-id header, include conversation_id. If connection drops, call resume endpoint with conversation state; server will replay up to the last confirmed token. If that doesn't exist, fallback is to re-issue a new generation with lower max_tokens for tail.

[03:52] Maya: You mentioned KV cache — is that customer-configurable or automatic? And does it persist across model versions?

[04:01] Marcus: It's automatic in hosted. We keep a short-lived prefix/KV cache (typical TTL 15 min by default) that speeds up autoregressive continuation. You can configure cache policies in Dedicated/Private to longer TTLs. It doesn't persist across incompatible model architecture changes — when you pin a different family or quantization level we invalidate relevant cache shards.

[04:30] Tom: What about cost—what levers do we have to reduce spend without increasing latency too much?

[04:39] Sofia: Good question. Common levers: lower max_tokens, use a smaller model for low-importance turns (we call this fallback routing), aggressive top_p/temperature constraints to reduce sampling, and batching for high-concurrency server endpoints. Also KV caching reduces emitted tokens — because you avoid regenerating the same prefix. There's also Redwood Optimize suggestions in the console which will recommend quantized variants and batching knobs based on sample traffic.

[05:12] Priya: Can you demo fallback to a cheaper model when latency spikes?

[05:17] Liam: Yep — switching to a small live demo. I'm going to simulate a latency spike on the primary model so you'll see automatic failover to a pinned fallback (gpt-small-ish alias in the sandbox).

[05:35] [05:38] (demo noise)

[05:40] Sofia: Notice the stream initially opens to Model A (higher perf). We're hitting an artificial capacity limit; Redwood's smart routing detects higher queueing latency and routes the next requests to Model B (cheaper). The client receives a short header that indicates fallback occurred so product analytics can mark degraded-quality responses.

[06:05] Maya: How do we measure quality degradation? Do you surface a score?

[06:12] Marcus: We have a quality baseline metric in Console called Q-Delta; you can define prompt sets and expected responses. When a fallback happens the Console will flag a regression if similarity drops below threshold. You can also hook evals to post-request sampling.

[06:34] Tom: Security — we need to ensure PHI doesn't leak. For hosted, is there tokenization or PII redaction? How is data retained?

[06:45] Sofia: Hosted default is short retention for logs and transcripts. For regulated data we recommend Dedicated or Private; Dedicated offers tenant isolation and optional log retention controls. For hosted, you can opt into zero-retention ingestion or enable encryption with customer-managed KMS for stored artifacts. We also provide audit logs and SSO/SAML for admin access.

[07:10] Evan: If we want to keep data in our VPC—what's the fastest path?

[07:16] Marcus: Private deployment (VPC or on-prem) is the path. We can run the same runtime in your environment; control plane can be customer-managed. We'll do a separate deep dive for networking and compliance.

[07:30] Liam: Back to the reconnect playbook — Sofia will walk through the common failure modes and recommended backoff.

[07:36] Sofia: Common failure modes: 1) short TCP disconnects (client-level reconnect), 2) server-side transient OOM/queueing (server retries + fallback), 3) partial payload loss (resume API), 4) idempotency mismatch (dedupe logic). Recommended pattern: optimistic streaming with incremental checkpoints — send a client ack every N tokens; on reconnect ask for suffix from last ack. Backoff: exponential (start 200ms, 2x up to 5s) plus jitter. If repeated failures, route to fallback model or degrade to sync response.

[08:28] Maya: The client ack — is that something Redwood enforces or a pattern we implement?

[08:33] Sofia: It's a client pattern. We expose the resume endpoint server-side and the conversation state can be requested by conversation_id. The server will reply with the last confirmed token index we have for that id.

[08:48] Priya: Any sample metrics we should surface in our product dashboard?

[08:53] Liam: Key metrics: latency p50/p95 for generations, stream connect success rate, resume success rate, fallback rate (percentage of requests routed to cheaper models), avg tokens per session, and cost per 1k tokens. Console will export these as CSV and allow alerting on thresholds.

[09:15] [09:18] (small crosstalk)

[09:20] Sofia: I'm going to paste the Node reconnect snippet into chat. Note we set header X-Redwood-Request-Id and conversation_id. On HEADERS mismatch you'll get a 409 indicating diverging state. The client should then fetch conversation state and reconcile.

[09:40] Maya: Are you doing anything special for partial message merges? We have users that expect messages to be stitched seamlessly if the client reconnects mid-token.

[09:49] Marcus: Stitching mid-token is tricky; we recommend trimming duplicates on the client side by tracking last confirmed token index. Tokens aren't always word boundaries so a small overlap is normal — trim by token index not by string match.

[10:12] Tom: How do retries interact with billing? If my client retries aggressively will that spike cost?

[10:18] Sofia: The platform dedupes identical request-ids for a short timeframe. If you're safe-retrying with the same id, you won't double-bill. If you issue a new request or change prompt, it's chargeable. For resume operations where you ask for the missing suffix (server-side), that is billed as additional tokens emitted only for the suffix that wasn't previously delivered.

[10:44] Priya: Let's talk about streaming chunk sizes. We saw earlier a parameter — what's the recommended tradeoff?

[10:52] Sophia (sic in transcript): chunk_size is client-side batching of tokens before flush. Larger chunks reduce network overhead (fewer packets) but increase latency for the first token. For chat UX you typically want small chunk_size (1-8 tokens) so first bytes arrive fast. For longer TTS or long-form content you can increase chunk_size.

[11:20] Evan: Does Redwood provide SDKs that implement these patterns?

[11:24] Liam: Yes — we have JS, Python, and Java SDKs with examples for streaming, reconnect, idempotency, and resumable sessions. We'll share the repo links in the follow-up.

[11:35] Maya: Can we see a quick end-to-end trace for a reconnect scenario?

[11:39] Sofia: Sure — demoing trace now. (screen) You can see the request flow: open stream -> tokens started -> disconnect at ~7s -> resume with same request-id -> server returns missing tokens -> client stitches and emits completion event. The trace shows p95 queueing spike which triggered a fallback in the next window.

[12:10] Tom: About the fallback — can we route only specific prompt types? For example: billing Q&A can use high-quality model but ephemeral chat tips can be cheaper?

[12:20] Marcus: Absolutely — routing policies are configurable by tag or route. You can include metadata like "policy: high_quality" in request headers and the router will prioritize latency/quality accordingly. We'll show how to set route tags in Console.

[12:45] Priya: Any gotchas for mobile clients?

[12:50] Sofia: Mobile has more flaky connectivity — use server-proxied streaming and short chunk sizes. For backgrounded apps switch to async notifications rather than long-lived sockets. Also consider token cost when sending large context from mobile — prefer server-side context enrichment.

[13:12] [13:15] (background noise)

[13:18] Liam: Quick note on safety — we do content filters and safety hooks. For hosted we apply standard safety checks; for enterprise you can bring your own safety model in Private.

[13:32] Maya: What about model pinning and version rollouts — can we canary a new model for 5% of traffic?

[13:40] Marcus: Yes. Console supports rollouts and A/B routing. You can pin versions, run a canary, and set automatic fallback if quality drops or latency exceeds SLO.

[13:55] Tom: Ok let's shift to the benchmark plan — we want to run a small test with 1k sessions, 3 messages each, measure p95 and avg token cost. What's the best way to do that?

[14:05] Liam: We'll provision a sandbox project. Use our load test harness in the samples repo which supports conversation patterns, token tracking, and automatic instrumentation for p50/p95 and cost. We'll also provide a spreadsheet template to capture results.

[14:22] Maya: Great — we'll run it with our redaction layer enabled to test PHI handling.

[14:29] Sofia: One last technical note on resumable tokens: if you have streaming with embedded tool calls (function calling), resume semantics are slightly different — the runtime will replay up to the call boundary, you should re-run the tool idempotently. We'll include the example for function/tool calls in the code snippets.

[14:55] Priya: Anything else we should be careful about?

[15:00] Marcus: Watch out for large context windows. If you always send entire conversation history on every request you'll inflate tokens fast; use summarized context or local client-side memory embeddings for retrieval. Redwood Optimize can suggest chunking and summarization points.

[15:18] Tom: Does Optimize do automatic batching suggestions?

[15:22] Liam: It will. Based on sample traffic it recommends batch sizes, quantization, and fallback thresholds to optimize cost without sacrificing SLOs.

[15:30] [15:33] (short silence)

[15:35] Liam: Wrapping up — recap and action items. We will provision sandbox access (Liam), Sofia will share reconnect/backoff code and Node/Python examples, Marcus will prep a private deployment checklist and pricing high-level, and Clearline will run the benchmark. We'll schedule a technical deep dive on Private & compliance next week.

[15:55] Tom: Sounds good. One ask — please include an offering matrix that compares Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private for compliance tradeoffs.

[16:03] Marcus: We'll include that in the technical deep dive packet.

[16:10] Maya: Thanks everyone — appreciate the demo.

[16:12] Liam: Thanks — we'll follow up with links and the snippet pack.

End meeting.
